title: Rethinking Evidence Modeling: Context-Coupled Graph Learning for Multimodal Recommendation

paper.title: Rethinking Evidence Modeling: Context-Coupled Graph Learning for Multimodal Recommendation
paper.abstract:
Abstract. Multimodal graph recommendation integrates observed interactions
with item images and text to learn user preferences. These inputs
constitute Semantic–Behavioral Evidence (SBE).
Many existing graph methods incorporate collaborative and
multimodal semantic relations, yet their aggregation and state
updates remain context-separated, limiting the continuous
composition of preference evidence across layers and the joint
use of multiple sources.
To address this limitation, we propose CC-MGRec , a context-coupled
graph learning method that organizes SBE within a common graph
learning context for cross-relation modeling and compositional
propagation.
Its context-coupled multimodal graph integrates user–item
collaborative relations and item–item semantic relations,
coordinating their message scales through joint normalization.
Recommendation-grounded semantic calibration uses training
behavior to adjust semantic neighbor weights while preserving
normalized collaborative propagation coefficients.
Collaborative–semantic compositional propagation updates shared
node states layer by layer to continuously compose collaborative
and multimodal semantic evidence, implicitly forming Preference
Evidence Chains (PECs), including collaborative–semantic and
visual–textual PECs.
Joint execution of relation messages on the same shared node
states within each layer preserves propagation outputs while
reducing intermediate output processing and fusion overhead.
We provide theoretical analysis of the proposed mechanisms.
Experiments on three Amazon datasets demonstrate improved
recommendation quality and faster inference during graph propagation.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Multimodal graph recommendation expresses SBE as node information and graph relations, and forms preference representations through propagation and fusion ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . At the representation level, VBPR incorporates visual content into preference representations, MMGCN learns modality-specific representations on the interaction graph, and SG-URInit constructs model-agnostic user initializations from historical item features and cluster information ( He and McAuley, 2016 ; Wei et al., 2019 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . UGT jointly optimizes image–text feature extraction and recommendation learning, aggregating multimodal content and ID information on the interaction graph ( Yi and Ounis, 2024 ) . Evidence modeling also organizes graph relations and state updates. GRCN refines observed interactions using content–preference agreement; LATTICE and FREEDOM construct content-derived item graphs, while DualGNN introduces user associations ( Wei et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Zhou and Shen, 2023 ; Wang et al., 2021 ) . In rating-feedback settings, SiMGR represents interactions through positive and negative relation graphs ( Lian et al., 2026 ) . For state updates, MIG-GT maintains modality-specific node states and receptive fields on the same interaction graph, whereas DHMRec passes interaction-graph states into subsequent item-graph learning ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhan et al., 2026 ) . These studies enrich evidence content, associations, and fusion strategies. Yet does expressing diverse evidence as node information and graph relations suffice for evidence carried by different relations to compose continuously across layers and jointly support preference learning? To answer this question, we examine the learning environment formed by node information, weighted relation neighborhoods, normalization, and state updates, which we term the graph learning context ( He et al., 2020 ) . Among representative designs using both collaborative and item–item semantic relations, fusion, alignment, or stage-wise transfer connects modality-specific or relation-specific state streams. The two relation types do not jointly update the same evolving node states at every layer. We refer to this organization as context-separated . Figure 1 contrasts learning from the same SBE under separate and coupled contexts. The illustrated separate context maintains relation-specific node states. In a context-coupled organization, collaborative and semantic relations jointly determine message scales through joint normalization and update shared node states at every layer. Evidence aggregated through one relation can therefore continue through other relations in subsequent layers. We use Preference Evidence Chains (PECs) to denote ordered, weighted propagation contributions implicitly formed by multilayer graph learning and incorporated into recommendation representations. Relative to the illustrated separate context, shared node-state updates retain within-relation PECs and support two additional compositions. Collaborative–semantic PECs (C–S PECs) allow interaction evidence to continue through item semantic relations and semantic evidence to re-enter collaborative learning. Visual–textual PECs (V–T PECs) allow evidence aggregated through one modality’s relations to continue through the other, composing the item connections revealed by both modalities. Two preliminary diagnostics examine the recommendation value of these compositions. C–S PEC support formed from training interactions and the pre-calibration semantic graph covers 10.84% of held-out positives on Baby versus 1.32% of matched unseen controls (Figure 2 (a)). In fixed trained models, removing V–T PEC contributions while retaining constituent evidence, relation support, and single-modality paths produces the largest ranking losses in high-exposure groups; some low-exposure groups change little or improve (Figure 2 (b)). These support-coverage differences and within-model ranking effects provide preliminary empirical motivation for supporting useful evidence compositions. Figure 1. From SBE to PECs under context-separated and context-coupled graph learning. Gold highlights the additional C–S and V–T PECs relative to the illustrated separate context. The schematic shows paired visual and textual item evidence and user interaction histories. Context-separated graph learning maintains distinct node states, whereas context-coupled graph learning shares states across collaborative and semantic relations. Five example PECs use chain links to trace visual, textual, and interaction SBE, highlighting additional collaborative–semantic and visual–textual PECs. The coupled context supports joint execution with less intermediate overhead. The second panel shows Hit@20 with minus without visual--textual PEC contributions in fixed models, grouped by pre-removal exposure. Error bars show user-clustered 95 percent confidence intervals. Figure 2. Preliminary diagnostics of PEC composition. (a) C–S PEC support coverage of held-out positives and matched unseen controls on Baby, using training interactions and the pre-calibration semantic graph. (b) Hit@20 differences (with minus without V–T PEC contributions) in fixed models, grouped by pre-removal exposure. Error bars indicate user-clustered 95% confidence intervals. The first panel compares collaborative–semantic PEC support coverage of held-out positives and matched unseen controls on Baby. The second panel shows Hit@20 with minus without visual–textual PEC contributions in fixed models, grouped by pre-removal exposure. Error bars show user-clustered 95 percent confidence intervals. Motivated by these observations, we propose Context-Coupled Graph Learning , implemented by CC-MGRec , which organizes SBE into a common graph learning context through graph construction, semantic calibration, and compositional propagation. Context-Coupled Multimodal Graph Construction ( CC-MG ) organizes node information and weighted relations from multimodal content and training behavior, jointly normalizing collaborative and semantic relations. Under joint normalization, semantic reweighting can also alter collaborative propagation coefficients. Recommendation-Grounded Semantic Calibration ( RGSC ) reallocates semantic neighbor weights using training behavior while preserving normalized collaborative propagation coefficients, with collaborative relations and other construction settings fixed. Collaborative–Semantic Compositional Propagation ( CSCP ) then updates shared node states layer by layer to implicitly form and aggregate C–S and V–T PECs. Shared states also support joint execution of relation messages. For identical relation operators and current-layer input states, a single assembled sparse operator produces outputs equivalent to relation-wise computation followed by summation, while reducing intermediate output accesses, fusion operations, and operator calls during graph-propagation inference. On Amazon Baby, Sports, and Clothing, CC-MGRec achieves the highest mean Recall and NDCG among the compared models and faster graph-propagation inference than MIG-GT. Our contributions are: • We propose CC-MGRec , a context-coupled graph learning framework that uses joint normalization and shared node-state updates to continuously compose SBE across layers, with C–S and V–T PECs characterizing cross-relation and cross-modal propagation contributions. • We develop recommendation-grounded semantic calibration that preserves normalized collaborative propagation coefficients, and output-equivalent joint execution that reduces relation-level intermediate output accesses and fusion overhead. • We analyze evidence composition, calibration invariance, and execution equivalence, and evaluate recommendation quality and graph-propagation inference efficiency on three datasets. Preliminary diagnostics, retrained mechanism controls, and output-equivalent execution experiments test the corresponding mechanisms.

sections.heading: 2.1. Multimodal Recommendation
sections.text: Multimodal recommendation extracts complementary preference evidence from item content and user behavior ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Images and text describe item appearance, attributes, and usage, observed interactions reflect behavioral preferences ( Liu et al., 2021 ) , and behavioral co-occurrence reveals user or item associations supported by common interactions. VBPR and ACF incorporate content into preference representations ( He and McAuley, 2016 ; Chen et al., 2017 ) . SLMRec, MMSSL, and BM3 enhance multimodal representations through self-supervised learning ( Tao et al., 2022 ; Wei et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ) , while SMORE improves representation quality through spectrum-based denoising and modality fusion ( Ong and Khong, 2025 ) . Evidence utilization also extends to input augmentation, initialization, and behavioral association modeling. SG-URInit constructs user initializations from historical item features and group information ( Xu et al., 2026 ) ; MLLMRec enhances preference reasoning with multimodal large language models ( Dang et al., 2026 ) ; GRE-MC completes missing modalities through graph retrieval ( Li et al., 2026b ) . DualGNN uses common interactions to establish user associations ( Wang et al., 2021 ) , IGDMRec incorporates item co-occurrence information to refine semantic relations ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , and BRIDGE uses behavior to calibrate candidate scores ( Li et al., 2026c ) . These studies enrich the evidence used for preference learning and the ways in which it is exploited ( Peng et al., 2025 ) .

LATTICE, MICRO, FREEDOM, and MGCN introduce item semantic relations ( Zhang et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ; Zhou and Shen, 2023 ; Yu et al., 2023 ) ; LGMRec and DOGE further incorporate higher-order structures ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Meng et al., 2025 ) . In rating-feedback settings, SiMGR distinguishes positive and negative interaction relations ( Lian et al., 2026 ) . Propagation organization determines how evidence carried by different relations participates in state updates. MMGCN and MIG-GT use modality-specific propagation ( Wei et al., 2019 ; Hu et al., 2025 ) , whereas CRANE, MGCN, and DHMRec connect collaborative and semantic learning through staged updates ( Dai et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2023 ; Zhan et al., 2026 ) . UGT unifies multimodal feature learning on the interaction graph ( Yi and Ounis, 2024 ) , while SCALE learns collaborative and semantic representations separately and connects them through alignment and fusion ( Li et al., 2026a ) . These studies organize evidence through different graph construction and propagation choices. From the perspective of PECs, existing structures support different forms of evidence composition. MGCN and DHMRec support C–S PECs through cross-relation state transfer ( Yu et al., 2023 ; Zhan et al., 2026 ) , while the merged semantic relations in LATTICE and FREEDOM support V–T PECs at sufficient propagation depth ( Zhang et al., 2021 ; Zhou and Shen, 2023 ) . Graph learning research also addresses propagation efficiency ( Besta and Hoefler, 2024 ) . HAGs reduce redundant computation through aggregation reuse ( Jia et al., 2020 ) , while Hector and TLV-HGNN optimize relational graph computation ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Han et al., 2025 ) . Our CC-MGRec organizes multimodal content, observed interactions, and behavioral co-occurrence information within a common graph learning context to support continuous evidence composition across relations and efficient inference.

sections.heading: 4.1. Framework Overview
sections.text: CC-MG is the core of CC-MGRec : it organizes multimodal node information and weighted collaborative and semantic relations in a shared graph learning context (Figure 3 ). RGSC refines semantic neighbor weights using training behavior while preserving their incoming budgets. CC-MG combines these calibrated connections with semantic node anchors and weighted interactions, then jointly normalizes the resulting graph. CSCP learns from this graph through one evolving node state, enabling cross-relation composition in a single propagation stream. sections.heading: 4.3. Context-Coupled Multimodal Graph Construction
sections.text: CC-MG organizes node information, relation connectivity, and relation strength for learning in one propagation stream. Visual and textual neighborhoods supply semantic connections; behavioral agreement determines their modality contributions, and RGSC calibrates individual neighbor weights. Semantic anchors provide node information and also guide interaction weighting. The weighted relations are assembled and jointly normalized into a common propagation operator. Together, these choices determine what recommendation evidence is available and how it enters the shared node state.

sections.heading: 4.4. Collaborative–Semantic Compositional Propagation
sections.text: We extend LightGCN ( He et al., 2020 ) to CC-MG through multimodal initialization and collaborative–semantic propagation. CSCP jointly updates shared node states with both relation families at each layer. This shared-state update enables cross-relation composition; the assembled operator evaluates the updates in a single propagation stream.

sections.heading: Collaborative–semantic updates.
sections.text: Each layer updates users from their interacted items and items from both users and semantic neighbors. Let 𝐇 𝒰 ( l ) \mathbf{H}_{\mathcal{U}}^{(l)} and 𝐇 ℐ ( l ) \mathbf{H}_{\mathcal{I}}^{(l)} denote the user and item states at layer l l , initialized by Eq. 10 . The user–item and item–item blocks of 𝐀 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{A}} are denoted by 𝐂 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{C}} and 𝐒 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{S}} , respectively. The user update is (15) 𝐇 𝒰 ( l + 1 ) = 𝐂 ^ ​ 𝐇 ℐ ( l ) . \mathbf{H}_{\mathcal{U}}^{(l+1)}=\widehat{\mathbf{C}}\mathbf{H}_{\mathcal{I}}^{(l)}. The item update combines collaborative and semantic messages: (16) 𝐇 ℐ ( l + 1 ) = 𝐂 ^ ⊤ ​ 𝐇 𝒰 ( l ) + 𝐒 ^ ​ 𝐇 ℐ ( l ) . \mathbf{H}_{\mathcal{I}}^{(l+1)}=\widehat{\mathbf{C}}^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{\mathcal{U}}^{(l)}+\widehat{\mathbf{S}}\mathbf{H}_{\mathcal{I}}^{(l)}. Here the first term aggregates user preferences along weighted interactions, and the second aggregates item information along calibrated semantic relations. Both use CC-MG’s joint normalization and the same preceding node state. Shared-state updates carry recommendation evidence across relation types. User information arriving at an item can reach semantic neighbors in the next layer, while semantically enriched item states can flow back to users. Deeper updates extend these collaborative–semantic paths. Within the semantic block, visual and textual relation contributions act on the same item states and can compose across layers to form V–T PECs.

sections.heading: Joint execution.
sections.text: A single sparse multiplication evaluates the user and item updates together. The assembled operator directly produces the next joint state, combining collaborative and semantic messages in one sparse operation per layer. It avoids separately materializing and merging relation outputs.

sections.heading: 6.1.1. Datasets and Evaluation
sections.text: We use Amazon Baby, Sports, and Clothing with MIG-GT’s filtered data and pre-extracted visual/textual features ( Hu et al., 2025 ) (Table 3 ). We follow its 8:1:1 split and full-ranking protocol, reporting Recall and NDCG at 10 and 20. Validation Recall@20 guides model selection and early stopping; graph construction, semantic anchors, and calibration use training interactions only.

sections.heading: 6.1.2. Baselines
sections.text: We compare two categories of baselines in Table 2 . The first uses only user–item interactions: MF ( Koren et al., 2009 ) , LightGCN ( He et al., 2020 ) , ApeGNN ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , and MGDN ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . The second combines interactions with item modality features: VBPR ( He and McAuley, 2016 ) , MMGCN ( Wei et al., 2019 ) , GRCN ( Wei et al., 2020 ) , DualGNN ( Wang et al., 2021 ) , SLMRec ( Tao et al., 2022 ) , LATTICE ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) , FREEDOM ( Zhou and Shen, 2023 ) , MIG-GT ( Hu et al., 2025 ) , and DHMRec ( Zhan et al., 2026 ) . Reproduced and compatible published results follow the same benchmark protocol.

sections.heading: 6.1.3. Implementation Details
sections.text: We use MIG-GT’s fixed modality projections ( Hu et al., 2025 ) , 128-dimensional embeddings, a batch size of 8,000, and an RTX 3090. Main results average five seeds; other experiments use three unless specified. Ablations use paired seeds, fixed context–target folds, matched initialization schemes, capacity, and training budgets. sections.text: Table 2 shows that CC-MGRec achieves the highest reported mean scores across all datasets and cutoffs. Improvements in both Recall and NDCG indicate gains in retrieval coverage and rank-sensitive quality. On Sports, relative gains are larger for shorter recommendation lists. The gains over MIG-GT and DHMRec support the framework’s ranking quality against the compared modality-specific and staged designs.

sections.text: Figure 5 shows that Full outperforms Raw in both recommendation metrics on every dataset. sections.heading: 7. Conclusion
sections.text: CC-MGRec organizes SBE within a shared graph learning context for multimodal recommendation, supporting semantic connectivity and C–S and V–T PEC composition. CC-MG jointly normalizes collaborative and semantic relations; RGSC calibrates semantic neighbors while preserving normalized collaborative propagation coefficients; and CSCP updates shared node states across layers. Experiments on three Amazon datasets demonstrate improved ranking over the compared baselines. Controlled comparisons support semantic connectivity beyond node information, C–S PEC composition beyond relation-pure propagation, and behavioral calibration. The output-equivalent R2/Joint control shows that joint execution reduces inference time while preserving propagation outputs. Timing covers fixed-weight graph propagation, excluding feature preparation, graph construction, calibration, and training.

Multimodal graph recommendation integrates observed interactions with item images and text to learn user preferences. These inputs constitute Semantic–Behavioral Evidence (SBE). Many existing graph methods incorporate collaborative and multimodal semantic relations, yet their aggregation and state updates remain context-separated, limiting the continuous composition of preference evidence across layers and the joint use of multiple sources. To address this limitation, we propose CC-MGRec , a context-coupled graph learning method that organizes SBE within a common graph learning context for cross-relation modeling and compositional propagation. Its context-coupled multimodal graph integrates user–item collaborative relations and item–item semantic relations, coordinating their message scales through joint normalization. Recommendation-grounded semantic calibration uses training behavior to adjust semantic neighbor weights while preserving normalized collaborative propagation coefficients. Collaborative–semantic compositional propagation updates shared node states layer by layer to continuously compose collaborative and multimodal semantic evidence, implicitly forming Preference Evidence Chains (PECs), including collaborative–semantic and visual–textual PECs. Joint execution of relation messages on the same shared node states within each layer preserves propagation outputs while reducing intermediate output processing and fusion overhead. We provide theoretical analysis of the proposed mechanisms. Experiments on three Amazon datasets demonstrate improved recommendation quality and faster inference during graph propagation. Keywords: Multimodal recommendation, evidence modeling, context-coupled graph learning, preference evidence chains 1. Introduction Multimodal graph recommendation expresses SBE as node information and graph relations, and forms preference representations through propagation and fusion ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . At the representation level, VBPR incorporates visual content into preference representations, MMGCN learns modality-specific representations on the interaction graph, and SG-URInit constructs model-agnostic user initializations from historical item features and cluster information ( He and McAuley, 2016 ; Wei et al., 2019 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . UGT jointly optimizes image–text feature extraction and recommendation learning, aggregating multimodal content and ID information on the interaction graph ( Yi and Ounis, 2024 ) . Evidence modeling also organizes graph relations and state updates. GRCN refines observed interactions using content–preference agreement; LATTICE and FREEDOM construct content-derived item graphs, while DualGNN introduces user associations ( Wei et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Zhou and Shen, 2023 ; Wang et al., 2021 ) . In rating-feedback settings, SiMGR represents interactions through positive and negative relation graphs ( Lian et al., 2026 ) . For state updates, MIG-GT maintains modality-specific node states and receptive fields on the same interaction graph, whereas DHMRec passes interaction-graph states into subsequent item-graph learning ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhan et al., 2026 ) . These studies enrich evidence content, associations, and fusion strategies. Yet does expressing diverse evidence as node information and graph relations suffice for evidence carried by different relations to compose continuously across layers and jointly support preference learning? To answer this question, we examine the learning environment formed by node information, weighted relation neighborhoods, normalization, and state updates, which we term the graph learning context ( He et al., 2020 ) . Among representative designs using both collaborative and item–item semantic relations, fusion, alignment, or stage-wise transfer connects modality-specific or relation-specific state streams. The two relation types do not jointly update the same evolving node states at every layer. We refer to this organization as context-separated . Figure 1 contrasts learning from the same SBE under separate and coupled contexts. The illustrated separate context maintains relation-specific node states. In a context-coupled organization, collaborative and semantic relations jointly determine message scales through joint normalization and update shared node states at every layer. Evidence aggregated through one relation can therefore continue through other relations in subsequent layers. We use Preference Evidence Chains (PECs) to denote ordered, weighted propagation contributions implicitly formed by multilayer graph learning and incorporated into recommendation representations. Relative to the illustrated separate context, shared node-state updates retain within-relation PECs and support two additional compositions. Collaborative–semantic PECs (C–S PECs) allow interaction evidence to continue through item semantic relations and semantic evidence to re-enter collaborative learning. Visual–textual PECs (V–T PECs) allow evidence aggregated through one modality’s relations to continue through the other, composing the item connections revealed by both modalities. Two preliminary diagnostics examine the recommendation value of these compositions. C–S PEC support formed from training interactions and the pre-calibration semantic graph covers 10.84% of held-out positives on Baby versus 1.32% of matched unseen controls (Figure 2 (a)). In fixed trained models, removing V–T PEC contributions while retaining constituent evidence, relation support, and single-modality paths produces the largest ranking losses in high-exposure groups; some low-exposure groups change little or improve (Figure 2 (b)). These support-coverage differences and within-model ranking effects provide preliminary empirical motivation for supporting useful evidence compositions. Figure 1. Motivated by these observations, we propose Context-Coupled Graph Learning , implemented by CC-MGRec , which organizes SBE into a common graph learning context through graph construction, semantic calibration, and compositional propagation. Context-Coupled Multimodal Graph Construction ( CC-MG ) organizes node information and weighted relations from multimodal content and training behavior, jointly normalizing collaborative and semantic relations. Under joint normalization, semantic reweighting can also alter collaborative propagation coefficients. Recommendation-Grounded Semantic Calibration ( RGSC ) reallocates semantic neighbor weights using training behavior while preserving normalized collaborative propagation coefficients, with collaborative relations and other construction settings fixed. Collaborative–Semantic Compositional Propagation ( CSCP ) then updates shared node states layer by layer to implicitly form and aggregate C–S and V–T PECs. Shared states also support joint execution of relation messages. For identical relation operators and current-layer input states, a single assembled sparse operator produces outputs equivalent to relation-wise computation followed by summation, while reducing intermediate output accesses, fusion operations, and operator calls during graph-propagation inference. On Amazon Baby, Sports, and Clothing, CC-MGRec achieves the highest mean Recall and NDCG among the compared models and faster graph-propagation inference than MIG-GT. Our contributions are: • We propose CC-MGRec , a context-coupled graph learning framework that uses joint normalization and shared node-state updates to continuously compose SBE across layers, with C–S and V–T PECs characterizing cross-relation and cross-modal propagation contributions. • We develop recommendation-grounded semantic calibration that preserves normalized collaborative propagation coefficients, and output-equivalent joint execution that reduces relation-level intermediate output accesses and fusion overhead. • We analyze evidence composition, calibration invariance, and execution equivalence, and evaluate recommendation quality and graph-propagation inference efficiency on three datasets. Preliminary diagnostics, retrained mechanism controls, and output-equivalent execution experiments test the corresponding mechanisms. 2. Related Work 2.1. Multimodal Recommendation Multimodal recommendation extracts complementary preference evidence from item content and user behavior ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Images and text describe item appearance, attributes, and usage, observed interactions reflect behavioral preferences ( Liu et al., 2021 ) , and behavioral co-occurrence reveals user or item associations supported by common interactions. VBPR and ACF incorporate content into preference representations ( He and McAuley, 2016 ; Chen et al., 2017 ) . SLMRec, MMSSL, and BM3 enhance multimodal representations through self-supervised learning ( Tao et al., 2022 ; Wei et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ) , while SMORE improves representation quality through spectrum-based denoising and modality fusion ( Ong and Khong, 2025 ) . Evidence utilization also extends to input augmentation, initialization, and behavioral association modeling. SG-URInit constructs user initializations from historical item features and group information ( Xu et al., 2026 ) ; MLLMRec enhances preference reasoning with multimodal large language models ( Dang et al., 2026 ) ; GRE-MC completes missing modalities through graph retrieval ( Li et al., 2026b ) . DualGNN uses common interactions to establish user associations ( Wang et al., 2021 ) , IGDMRec incorporates item co-occurrence information to refine semantic relations ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , and BRIDGE uses behavior to calibrate candidate scores ( Li et al., 2026c ) . These studies enrich the evidence used for preference learning and the ways in which it is exploited ( Peng et al., 2025 ) . 2.2.
